grammar.en: 'Waiting.' Since smartphones spread, we have become bad at waiting. Even during a few minutes waiting for a train, we can't help looking at the screen. In this way, boring time seems to have vanished completely from our lives. But is waiting really wasted time? As a child I waited many days for letters from my grandmother, who lived far away. I imagined all sorts of things: what is she doing now, did my letter make her laugh? I think it was because I had that waiting time that I read her letters again and again. Now a reply comes seconds after you send a message. It is certainly more convenient. But many people feel anxious or get angry when a reply does not come right away. reading.en: When we see beautiful scenery on a trip, we take out our smartphones at once. One shot, then another from a different angle. Before we know it, we have spent more time looking at the screen than at the view itself. There is a psychology experiment: visitors to an art museum were split into two groups; one could photograph the works freely, the other could only look. The next day, when tested on how much they remembered, the group that took photos had vaguer memories. The researchers think the feeling of security from having photos may make the brain think 'I don't need to remember'. Hearing this, I was strangely convinced. I have hundreds of photos of the sea from a family trip a few years ago, yet I can hardly recall what we talked about or what the wind was like. On the other hand, I vividly remember small scenes from childhood summers when I had no camera. Of course, I am not saying photos are bad. Memory fades with time, and photos are clues to bring it back. The problem is when taking photos becomes the goal and looking is neglected. A record cannot replace memory. Records are useful only when there was a real experience first. Recently I made a rule for trips: when I meet something beautiful, I first look at it for one minute without doing anything. Only then do I take a photo. Even one minute leaves the light, the sounds around me and what I felt strangely clear in my heart. And when I look back at the photos later, I can remember even things that are not in them.

reading.en: There has probably never been an age that loves the word 'efficiency' so much. In work and study, people are judged on how quickly they get results. Bookshops are full of books promising results 'in the shortest way' or 'in one week', and young people seem to fear detours more than anything. I have supervised research at a university for many years, and recent students are very capable. Give them a task and they quickly gather materials and summarize them neatly. But many of them freeze in front of a question with no answer. They don't know where to start. That is not surprising. They have been taught the shortest route to the correct answer, and have hardly ever walked where there is no road. Research is by nature a series of detours: form a hypothesis, experiment, fail, form it again. In trial and error that looks wasteful in hindsight, researchers develop the eye to see a subject from many sides. People who have only walked the shortest road may reach their goal but don't know the land around it, so once they leave the road they don't know where they are. To avoid misunderstanding: I don't reject seeking efficiency itself. Getting results in limited time is an essential skill in society. The problem is when efficiency becomes the only measure and detours are simply labeled 'bad'. I want young people sometimes to take detours on purpose: think with your own head before looking up the answer; read a book you don't know will be useful. Such seemingly wasted time should strengthen the legs you need to face questions without answers.
